title: The Lot on Elm Street
tagline: A $2M grant and a vacant lot in Eastside. Who decides what gets built?

lines.text: Riverton City Hall. A grant check for $2 million sits on the table, and a vacant lot on Elm Street in Eastside sits empty a few miles away.
Welcome to your first big decision as a youth commissioner. The lot has been vacant for eleven years. This grant is a chance to do something with it.
Eastside has the shortest life expectancy in the city. Whatever we build, we have to build it with the people who live there, not for them.
I should start with the facts before I decide whom to ask.

nodes.title: Eastside by the numbers
nodes.intro: Here is how Eastside compares with the rest of Riverton. Look at the gaps before you decide who to listen to.
nodes.question: q-xr-data

nodes.prompt: You will hold a listening session before the commission votes. How and when will you hold it?

choices.label: A weekday evening at City Hall
choices.detail: 6 p.m. Tuesday. Easy for staff to run. Parking downtown.

choices.label: A Saturday at the Eastside community center
choices.detail: With childcare, interpreters, and food. More work to organize.

choices.label: Post an online survey and skip the meeting
choices.detail: Fast and cheap. Anyone with a phone and time can answer.

nodes.prompt: Think about who can actually show up. For each person, who is likely to benefit from your choice, who is likely to bear a cost, and who is likely to be left out?

lines.text: At 6 p.m. the hall is half empty. Most of the people in the seats are city staff, retirees, and the developer's team.
We have good people here, but I do not see many families from Eastside.
Of course. A Tuesday evening downtown is hard if you work two jobs or have no car.
Saturday at the Eastside community center. Kids color in one corner, interpreters wear bright vests, and the room smells like fresh tamales.
I came because there is childcare. I could not have made a weekday meeting.
First time anyone asked me anything about this street in forty years.
The online survey gets 212 responses in a week. A quick look at the zip codes shows most are from outside Eastside.
Good response rate. But who did we hear from?
People with fast internet and spare time. Eastside has the lowest home internet access in the city.

nodes.prompt: Time is short. Whom will you listen to?

stakeholders.name: Mr. Walter Whitfield
stakeholders.needs: A grocery nearby and a safe place to walk.

lines.text: When I moved here there was a grocery on this corner. Now the closest real store is a bus ride away.
My sugar runs high. The doctor says walk more. Where? The park is dark at night and the sidewalks are broken.
Build something for the people who are already here.

stakeholders.fact: Eastside diabetes is 15.5%, compared with 6.2% in Hillcrest.

stakeholders.name: Ms. Rosa Alvarez
stakeholders.needs: A clinic open evenings and weekends, close to home.

lines.text: My son has asthma. When he has an attack at 9 p.m., the clinic is closed, so we go to the ER and wait four hours.
I took a Saturday because there is childcare. Please do not decide everything at a meeting I cannot attend.
Something close that is open when I am off work would change our lives.

stakeholders.fact: Preventable ER visits are 142 per 1,000 in Eastside, compared with 38 in Hillcrest.

stakeholders.name: Mr. Daniel Park
stakeholders.needs: A plan that does not wipe out local businesses.

lines.text: I have sold milk and bread on Elm Street for twenty years. A big co-op could take my customers.
But if it hires neighbors and stocks my produce, I would partner. I want to be at the table, not on the menu.

stakeholders.fact: Corner stores can convert to healthy-food stores with small grants.

stakeholders.name: Pastor Grace Bell
stakeholders.needs: Protection from rising rents after improvements arrive.

lines.text: Every time something nice comes to a neighborhood like ours, rents go up and families leave. I have married couples who now live forty minutes away.
If you build, protect the people already here. Otherwise it is a gift for someone else.

stakeholders.fact: Rent pressure often rises after new amenities open in lower-income areas.

stakeholders.name: Jordan Reyes
stakeholders.needs: A safe, free place to be active, and a real vote for young people.

lines.text: There is nowhere free and safe to hang out. My little brother stays inside with his inhaler.
We do not want another survey. We want a seat in the room.

stakeholders.fact: Eastside has the lowest park access of any Riverton neighborhood.

stakeholders.name: Dr. Mei Lin
stakeholders.needs: Steady funding for a satellite clinic with evening hours.

lines.text: My clinic has six-week waits. A small Eastside site with evening hours would keep many families out of the ER.
Equipment is a one-time cost. Staff are the long-term cost, and that needs a funding plan.

stakeholders.fact: Primary-care access lowers preventable ER visits.

stakeholders.name: Marcus Hale
stakeholders.needs: Financing that makes a project work.

lines.text: I can add $2 million to your grant. In exchange, I need market-rate apartments on part of the lot to make the numbers work.
That money builds more clinic and park than the grant alone. I am not your enemy; I just have to pay my investors.

stakeholders.fact: Market-rate housing near new amenities can raise nearby rents.

nodes.title: What people say, and what the data shows
nodes.prompt: Both count as evidence. Neither automatically wins. What does each tell you?

perceptions.quote: "What we really need is a big hospital."
"Kids here just do not eat right. It is a personal choice problem."
"Asthma is just something families here live with."

data.label: Preventable ER visits per 1,000
data.value: Eastside 142 vs. Hillcrest 38: most are for care that a nearby clinic could provide.

data.label: Food access index (0 to 100)
data.value: Eastside 22 vs. Hillcrest 88: no full-service grocery within walking distance.

data.label: Childhood asthma
data.value: Eastside 17.8% vs. Hillcrest 6.5%, with homes near the highway and factory.

nodes.prompt: Which evidence is shaping your thinking? Choose everything that matters to you.

lines.text: Before you build a proposal: the developer has put an offer in writing. $2 million more, in exchange for market-rate housing on part of the lot.
It doubles what you can build. It does change who lives next door to the new buildings.
More money is not automatically better. I need to ask who pays for it, and in what way.

nodes.prompt: Build your proposal for the Elm Street lot. The grant is $2.0M. The developer's offer adds $2.0M but includes market-rate housing.
Every proposal gives something up. What are you giving up?

options.label: Smaller buildings than residents asked for
Voices I did not have time to hear

nodes.prompt: Name one alternative you considered and say why you set it aside.
Does your proposal narrow or widen the health gap between Eastside and the rest of Riverton, and for whom?

lines.text: The commission meets at 8 p.m. The grant has a deadline, and three commissioners want to vote tonight.
I am inclined to support a plan that protects current residents. I want to know what happens to rents.
We can vote now, amend the proposal, or table it. The room is waiting.

nodes.prompt: The chair looks at you. The clock is running.

choices.label: Move to a vote on the proposal as written
Amend: add housing protections and a resident seat on the oversight board
Table the vote for two weeks to hear more residents
Build whatever gets the most votes
choices.detail: Rework the proposal on the spot to win over the loudest voices.

nodes.prompt: In one to three sentences, explain your choice to the room.
Pause and think. Without the clock, would you make the same move?

choices.label: Switch to: Move to a vote on the proposal as written
Switch to: Amend: add housing protections and a resident seat on the oversight board
Switch to: Table the vote for two weeks to hear more residents
Switch to: Build whatever gets the most votes
choices.detail: Rework the proposal on the spot to win over the loudest voices.

lines.text: Five years pass. Cranes, then ribbon-cuttings, then ordinary Tuesdays. Here is what happened on Elm Street.

nodes.prompt: Look at your projected results compared with what was typical. How should you judge how good your decision was?

ending.title: A shared table
ending.summary: The lot became a clinic, a market, and a park that residents helped design. The health gap narrowed and most longtime residents stayed.

lines.text: I walk to the market now. First time my legs and my sugar both thank me.
The clinic is open on Saturdays. My son has not been to the ER in a year.
They gave us a seat on the board. We use it.

ending.title: Progress, but whose neighborhood?
ending.summary: The buildings opened and conditions improved, but rents rose and many longtime residents moved away, so the people the project meant to help did not all benefit.

lines.text: Half my congregation now commutes to services from forty minutes away.
The new market is nice. I do not know a single person in the building next door.
Numbers say Eastside is healthier. It is partly because different people live here.

ending.title: A good plan nobody trusted
ending.summary: The projects opened, but many residents felt the decision was made without them, so use was low and the community stayed wary of the next proposal.

lines.text: I never heard back after the first survey. I do not know who it is for.
Nobody called me before they built next to my store.
Next time we need to start with relationships, not announcements.

ending.title: Mixed results
ending.summary: Some things improved and some did not. The health gap narrowed a little, trust held steady, and the community is cautiously hopeful.

lines.text: Better than nothing, and a lot better than eleven years of weeds.
It helps. I wish it had been bigger.
We will keep pushing.

ending.title: The vote falls short
ending.summary: The proposal did not get enough votes. Without a plan the commission could agree on, the lot stays empty another year.

lines.text: We could not agree, and Eastside pays for that every day the lot sits empty.
A decision that cannot win support is not a decision. We will try again.

ending.title: The grant slips away
ending.summary: Tabling the vote bought time to hear more residents, but the deadline passed. The $2 million was awarded to another city.

lines.text: Tabling was a reasonable call, and a risky one. Sometimes good judgment still meets bad luck.
So we wait again.

debrief.rubricNote: Your reasoning is scored, never your choice. There is no single right answer to a real trade-off.
